paperTitle: Singapore-Cambridge GCE O-Level 1184 English Language — AI-authored Practice 47: The Letter from Tekong (§B style, standard band)
provenanceNote: NOT STUDENT-FACING. Original narrative written for the morning-quiz bank; NOT from any past exam paper. Section B [19 marks], 1184/02 §B format, SEAB assessment objectives. 10 short-answer items (mixed [1]/[2]) + 4-blank emotion flowchart split for independent auto-grading.

sections.instruction: Read the narrative text below about a girl who receives letters from her older brother during his national service, and answer the questions that follow. Section B, Part 1 [15 marks]. Answer in your own words as far as possible.
sections.passage:
Paragraph 1
My brother Yong Han and I had not held a real conversation in about three years. This was not a quarrel. It was simply what had happened: he grew up, moved his desk into the storeroom, and began answering questions with the smallest number of syllables the question allowed.

Paragraph 2
Then he was enlisted, and they took his phone away for the first two weeks, and he wrote me a letter.

Paragraph 3
It arrived in a brown envelope with the address written in capitals, as though he did not trust his own handwriting to survive the journey. Inside were two pages. The first was about food. The second was not.

Paragraph 4
He wrote that on the third night he had been so tired that he had cried, quietly, in a room with eleven other men, and that nobody had noticed, and that he had been grateful for that and ashamed of it at the same time. He wrote that a boy in his section named Faizal had, without being asked, packed Yong Han's field pack for him one morning when Yong Han's hands were shaking too badly to do it.

Paragraph 5
I read it standing in the corridor. Then I read it again on the sofa. Then I put it in my drawer and did not tell our mother, because he had not written to her, and I understood without being told why he had not.

Paragraph 6
I wrote back the same evening. I filled four pages with nothing — the cat, a test I had failed, the fact that the lift in our block had broken again. I did not mention the crying. I understood that it had been given to me, not offered for discussion.

Paragraph 7
When he came home on his first weekend, he was thinner and stood differently. He said 'Hi' at the door and nothing else. At dinner he answered our mother in the same three-syllable way he always had. I thought, for one flat moment, that the letter had been a mistake, or a fever, or someone else.

Paragraph 8
Then, washing up, he said without turning round: 'You wrote back very fast.'

Paragraph 9
'Yes.'

Paragraph 10
'Okay,' he said. And that was the whole conversation, and it was enough, and I have thought about it many times since.

Paragraph 11
He writes less often now. But the drawer is not empty, and when I open it I am reminded that people are not only what they can manage to say out loud at the dinner table.

questions.stem: Q1. From Paragraph 1, how had Yong Han's behaviour towards his sister changed over three years? [1]
questions.answer: he had withdrawn, moving into the storeroom and replying in as few words as possible

questions.stem: Q2. Using your own words, explain why the narrator insists that the silence between them 'was not a quarrel'. (Paragraph 1) [2]
questions.answer: ① there had been no argument or bad feeling between them; ② the distance came simply from him growing older and more private, which she wants understood as ordinary rather than hostile

questions.stem: Q3. What does the detail of the address 'written in capitals' suggest about Yong Han? (Paragraph 3) [1]
questions.answer: that he took unusual care over the letter / wanted to be certain it reached her

questions.stem: Q4. What is the effect of the short sentence 'The second was not.' at the end of Paragraph 3? [2]
questions.answer: the abruptness marks the point where the letter turns serious and warns the reader that something more difficult is coming, making the contrast with the harmless first page sharper than an explanation would

questions.stem: Q5. Using your own words, explain why Yong Han felt both 'grateful' and 'ashamed' that nobody noticed him crying. (Paragraph 4) [2]
questions.answer: ① he was relieved that his distress had stayed private among strangers; ② he was humiliated that he had broken down at all, so the same fact both protected and embarrassed him

questions.stem: Q6. Why does the writer include the detail that Faizal acted 'without being asked'? (Paragraph 4) [1]
questions.answer: it shows the kindness was freely given and spared Yong Han having to admit he could not cope

questions.stem: Q7. Using your own words, explain why the narrator did not tell their mother about the letter. (Paragraph 5) [2]
questions.answer: ① he had chosen to write to her alone, and passing it on would betray that choice; ② she recognised he could not let their mother see him that vulnerable

questions.stem: Q8. What is the effect of the narrator filling four pages 'with nothing' in her reply? (Paragraph 6) [2]
questions.answer: the ordinary trivia is exactly the point — she answers his openness with normality rather than sympathy, giving him contact without forcing him to discuss what he had admitted

questions.stem: Q9. From Paragraph 7, give TWO ways in which Yong Han seemed unchanged at the dinner table. [1]
questions.answer: he greeted her with a single word and answered their mother in the same very short replies as before

questions.stem: Q10. Using your own words, explain why the exchange at the sink was 'enough' for the narrator. (Paragraph 10) [1]
questions.answer: it privately confirmed that the letter and her reply had mattered to him, without either having to say so directly
